newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S&P to visit S.Africa, rating seen held.
newsitem.headline: S&P to visit S.Africa, rating seen held.

text.p: Influential U.S. ratings agency Standard and Poor's is to visit South Africa next week for its annual review of the country, a Finance Ministry spokeswoman said on Friday.

Analysts said S&P was likely to maintain its rating of the country's foreign currency debt at BB+ -- one notch below investment grade -- when it published the findings of its review in October or November. Rand-denominated debt is rated BBB+.

"An improvement in the rating is highly unlikely given the past few months' disturbances on the financial markets. But we don't expect ratings to deteriorate either," said Magan Mistry, economist at Nedcor.
A major plus since the last S&P rating, issued on November 20, 1995, had been the publication of Finance Minister Trevor Manuel's market-orientated macro-economic strategy in June, economists said.
S&P itself praised the strategy as a consistent and coherent plan at the end of July.
A further positive was the success of local government elections, particularly in KwaZulu-Natal where polling in June passed off without the widepread bloodshed that had been feared.
But the plunge in the rand, leading to a fall in capital inflows, a widening current account deficit and a slide in official reserves, remained a major headache.
"After what has happened to our reserves, in particular, this year I would say an uprating is near impossible," said BOE NatWest strategic economist Nick Barnardt.
South African gold and foreign exchange reserves at end-August stood at 10.1 billion rand, representing just one month's import cover.
"But I don't see any risk of a downgrade. Policies are moving in the right direction, with a strict monetary policy and inflation declining from when they (S&P) were here last," Barnardt said.
South African consumer inflation has ticked up in recent months, reflecting the fall in the currency, but at 7.1 percent in July still remains below last August's level of 7.5 percent.
Peter Worthington, emerging market analyst at J.P. Morgan in London, agreed S&P would not act at present, but might upgrade after the next budget, due in March 1997.
"I'm inclined to think they will hold. But they may take a more positive stance after the next budget which will crystalise a lot of the detail of the economic plan," he said.

European credit rating agency IBCA, the first to reassess South africa's country risk following the rand slide which started last February, said in early June it was holding its long term foreign currency rating at BB. Local currency debt was assigned a BBB rarting.
Analysts noted this assessment was made before publication of the government's macro-economic strategy on June 14 and the peaceful KwaZulu-Natal elections on June 26.

Moody's Investors Services Inc was scheduled to visit South Africa next year, the Finance Ministry spokeswoman said. Moody's currently rates South Africa's foreign currency debt at an investment grade Baa3 and rand-denominated debt at Baa1.
